clinicalPearls: Defined by an early repolarisation pattern on the electrocardiogram together with otherwise unexplained ventricular arrhythmia or sudden cardiac arrest
The electrocardiographic pattern is J-point elevation with notching or slurring in the inferior or lateral leads
The early repolarisation pattern alone is extremely common and usually benign; it becomes a syndrome only with arrhythmic events
It belongs to the J-wave syndromes, sharing mechanistic overlap with Brugada syndrome
It should be distinguished from the benign pattern and from ischaemia and other causes of J-point elevation
Management of the syndrome may include an implantable defibrillator and isoproterenol or quinidine for electrical storm
reference.pathophysiology: Early repolarisation syndrome is thought to arise from heterogeneity of repolarisation between the epicardium and endocardium, related to a prominent transient outward potassium current that exaggerates the early repolarisation notch. This transmural dispersion of repolarisation creates a substrate for phase-2 re-entry and closely coupled ventricular ectopy that can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. The same electrocardiographic pattern occurs benignly in many healthy people, so the arrhythmic risk depends on additional factors and clinical context.
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram characterising the J-point changes
Assessment of the clinical context and any arrhythmic events
Exclusion of ischaemia and other causes of J-point elevation
Family assessment where a syndrome is confirmed
redFlags: Unexplained cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation with the pattern
High-risk electrocardiographic features (high-amplitude J waves, horizontal ST segments)
Family history of sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: The isolated pattern is benign in the vast majority; the syndrome, defined by arrhythmic events, carries a risk of recurrent life-threatening arrhythmia requiring definitive management.
pitfalls: Labelling the common benign pattern as a dangerous syndrome
Missing ischaemia or pericarditis as a cause of J-point changes
Underestimating risk when high-risk features and events coexist
Failing to assess the family after a confirmed syndrome
